name: Semmelweis on childbed fever (1847)
description: Ignaz Semmelweis's case that chlorine handwashing prevents puerperal fever, as he could have stated it in 1847, with the assumptions his inference rested on made explicit. Written to show how a scientific argument looks in this format: observations as foundations, a mechanism that is assumed rather than observed, and a practical ought at the end. Nothing here is an endorsement of the historical details as exact.

meta.note: Statements are in Semmelweis's first person. meta.role marks observations, hypotheses, assumptions, and rules. Modern germ theory is deliberately absent: the point is what his argument rested on at the time.
meta.sources: Semmelweis, Die Aetiologie, der Begriff und die Prophylaxis des Kindbettfiebers (1861), recounting the 1847 events; secondary accounts.

statements.text: In the First Clinic, where medical students deliver, mothers die of childbed fever far more often than in the Second Clinic, where midwives deliver.
The two clinics admit women from the same population, alternating by day of the week.
The cause of the extra deaths lies in something done differently in the First Clinic, not in the women.
Women who give birth in the street on the way to the hospital rarely develop the fever.
Medical students and their teachers come to the delivery ward straight from dissecting corpses.
Midwives never handle corpses.
My colleague Kolletschka died of a disease with the same course as childbed fever after a student's scalpel cut him during an autopsy.
Diseases with the same course have the same cause.

meta.note: A general principle Semmelweis relied on and never argued for. It is what lets the Kolletschka case bear on the mothers.

statements.text: Some matter from corpses, carried on the hands, causes the fever when it enters the body.

meta.note: The mechanism. Not observed; inferred. Bacteria were unknown to him.

statements.text: Ordinary washing with soap does not remove the cadaverous smell, so it does not remove the matter.

meta.note: Smell was his only indicator of the matter's presence.

statements.text: Washing in chlorinated lime removes the cadaverous smell from the hands.
Where the smell goes, the matter goes.

meta.note: Hidden premise linking the smell test to the causal agent.

statements.text: Washing in chlorinated lime removes the cadaverous matter from the hands.
If every examiner washed in chlorinated lime before examining a mother, the fever in the First Clinic would fall to the Second Clinic's level.
After I required chlorine washing in May 1847, mortality in the First Clinic fell to the level of the Second Clinic within months.
Nothing else about the First Clinic changed in those months.

meta.note: The uncontrolled-experiment assumption; the weakest point of the case as stated.

statements.text: Chlorine handwashing before examinations prevents childbed fever.
We physicians have been carrying the cause of death to the mothers on our own hands.
A physician must adopt any practice that prevents deaths among his patients.
Every physician and student must wash in chlorinated lime before examining a mother.

arguments.justification: If the same women, assigned by the calendar, die at different rates in the two clinics, the difference cannot be in the women; it must be in what each clinic does to them.

meta.note: Mill's method of difference, before Mill's name was attached to it in this context.

arguments.justification: Women who avoid the clinic's examinations altogether are safer than those examined in it, which again points at something done during the examinations.

meta.note: An independent second argument for the same conclusion. It stays separate rather than being merged into the first.

arguments.justification: Kolletschka's disease ran the course of childbed fever and was caused by corpse matter entering a wound; by the principle that the same course means the same cause, corpse matter entering the body is what causes the fever in mothers too.

The agent comes from corpses; the First Clinic's examiners handle corpses and the Second Clinic's do not; the difference between the clinics is what the examiners do. So the examiners' hands are the route.
Soap leaves the smell and therefore the matter; chlorine removes the smell, and the matter travels with the smell; so chlorine removes the matter.
If the hands carry the cause and chlorine washing clears the hands of it, then chlorine washing before every examination should stop the transmission.
The prediction was made, the practice was introduced, mortality fell as predicted, and nothing else changed. The fall is therefore due to the washing.

meta.note: Confirmation, not proof: the argument is only as strong as the assumption that nothing else changed.

arguments.justification: Washing prevents the deaths, and a physician must adopt what prevents deaths; therefore every examiner must wash.
